title: Holes in the prairie
teaches: Why central Whidbey has open prairies and pits with no outlets: gravel that drains too fast for young firs, blocks of buried ice, and thousands of years of fire

parts.title: Open ground on a forested island

blocks.text: Most of western Washington, left alone, grows forest: Douglas fir, western red cedar and hemlock, closing over within decades of any clearing. But on central Whidbey there are open prairies: Ebey’s Prairie behind Coupeville, Smith Prairie and Crockett Prairie, flat and treeless when the first American settlers arrived in the 1850s. The settlers ploughed them at once, and some of the farms are still worked by the same families.

Just west of Coupeville, along the Kettles Trail, the ground at the prairie’s edge, now mostly forest, is pocked with pits: hollows tens of metres across and up to 30 metres or so deep, with no stream running in or out. Rain falls into them and disappears. Some hold a small marsh at the bottom; most are dry.

blocks.caption: Ebey’s Prairie, open farmland on central Whidbey, with forest on the higher ground around it.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Central Whidbey has natural prairies, open when settlers arrived in the 1850s.
Near Coupeville the forest hides deep pits with no outlets.

blocks.text: Both puzzles start with the ground. The prairies and the pits lie on **outwash**: sand and gravel spread by meltwater as the Puget lobe melted back about 16,000 years ago, younger than the Esperance Sand that was spread as the ice advanced (the previous lesson tells the ice’s story here). The forest around them grows mostly on till and finer sediments. Outwash gravel has large pores; water runs through it in hours and leaves the stones nearly dry. Till and silt have small pores that hold water against gravity for weeks.

blocks.caption: The water a young tree’s roots can reach in the top 60 cm of each soil, as a dry summer goes on. The amounts are typical, not measured on Whidbey.
blocks.task: Run the dry spell until the gravel is dry but the till is not

blocks.text: Central Whidbey lies in the **rain shadow** of the Olympics: wet Pacific air drops most of its rain on the mountains’ western slopes and arrives here much drier. Coupeville gets only a small fraction of the rain of the Olympic rainforests, and its summers are dry. On the gravel, a young Douglas fir’s shallow roots run out of water within a few weeks of the last rain, and seedlings die. Grasses and wildflowers, which finish their growth by early summer and wait out the drought, do well. On the till, the seedlings survive.

The pits are **kettles**, the same as those in lesson 16. As the ice wasted away, blocks of it were stranded and buried by the outwash that meltwater was spreading around them. When the buried ice finally melted, the gravel above it collapsed into the hole. Lidar of the area shows dozens of them, lined up along the paths the meltwater took.

blocks.caption: Central Whidbey. Ebey’s Prairie lies between Coupeville and Ebey’s Landing; the Kettles lie nearby, toward Fort Ebey. Positions approximate.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The prairies sit on outwash gravel, which drains fast and dries out in summer.
Young firs die on the dry gravel; grasses survive.
The pits are kettles: holes left when buried blocks of ice melted.

blocks.text: Gravel alone may not be the whole answer. The prairies were also kept open by people. For centuries, and probably much longer, Coast Salish people, on central Whidbey the Lower Skagit, set fires on the prairies every few years. Fire killed fir seedlings and encouraged the plants they harvested, above all **camas**, a perennial herb whose bulbs were a staple food, dug and pit-roasted in large quantities.[^camas] Pollen and charcoal in lake and bog sediments on the island record open ground and fire going back thousands of years.

When the burning stopped in the nineteenth century, firs began to creep onto the edges of prairies all over the Puget Lowland, especially where the soil held a little more water. On central Whidbey, ploughing took over from fire. The prairie is a joint product of fast-draining gravel, dry summers and people who knew how to use both. Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve now protects the farms, the kettles and the bluff of the previous lesson together.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Coast Salish people burned the prairies for centuries or longer, keeping them open for camas.
When burning stopped, firs advanced; on Whidbey the plough replaced fire.

blocks.caption: Five questions on Whidbey’s prairies
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why do young Douglas firs struggle on outwash gravel?
choices: The gravel drains fast and dries out in the summer drought
items.why: Large pores let water drain in hours; a few rainless weeks leave the roots dry.

items.ask: Why do grasses manage where firs fail?
choices: They finish growing by early summer and wait out the drought
They have deeper roots than trees
items.why: Grasses and wildflowers grow in the wet spring and go dormant in the dry summer.

choices: Blocks of ice buried in outwash melted, and the ground collapsed into the holes
items.why: Stranded ice was buried by meltwater gravel; when it melted, the gravel fell in.

items.ask: What else kept the prairies open?
choices: Regular burning by Coast Salish people
items.why: Fire every few years killed fir seedlings and favoured camas and other food plants.

items.ask: What happened when the burning stopped?
choices: Firs began to spread onto the prairie edges
items.why: Without fire, seedlings survive where the soil holds enough water.

summary: **Whidbey has natural prairies.** Open ground on a forested island.
**They lie on outwash gravel.** Meltwater spread it as the ice melted back.
**Gravel drains fast.** In a dry summer young firs run out of water.
**The pits are kettles.** Buried ice melted and the gravel collapsed.
**People kept the prairies open.** Coast Salish burning favoured camas.
**When fire stopped, firs advanced.** On Whidbey, farming took over.
**The prairie is a joint product.** Geology, climate and people together.

camas.title: Camas
camas.text: Common camas (Camassia quamash) has blue flowers that, in spring, could make a prairie look like a lake. Its bulbs, slow-roasted for a day or more in earth ovens, turn sweet. Prairies were tended and harvested by families who held rights to particular patches, and the fires were part of that tending.
